evidence_spans: At low temperatures, due to high surface energy, single element metallic nanowires such as Ag usually transform into a more preferred phase via nucleation and propagation of partial dislocation through the nanowire, enabling superplasticity.
The results demonstrate that Ag nanowires exhibit apparent temperature-dependent superplasticity at cryogenic temperature due to (110) to (100) cross-section reorientation behavior.

defects: partial dislocation motion hindered by friction

evidence_spans: In high entropy alloy (HEA) CoNiCrFeMn nanowires, the motion of the partial dislocation is hindered by the friction due to difference in the lattice parameter of the constituent atoms which is responsible for the hardening and lowering the ductility.

intervention.description: molecular dynamics simulations at cryogenic temperatures

evidence_units.mechanism: synergistic interactions of deformation twinning, FCC-HCP phase transformation, and the special reorientation of the cross-section
evidence_spans: Interestingly, HEA nanowires can perform exceptional strength-ductility trade-offs at cryogenic temperatures.

Mechanical properties of HEA nanowires are better than Ag nanowires due to synergistic interactions of deformation twinning, FCC-HCP phase transformation, and the special reorientation of the cross-section.

intervention.description: molecular dynamics simulations at high temperatures

evidence_units.mechanism: simultaneous activation of twining induced plasticity and transformation induced plasticity
evidence_spans: Even at high temperatures, HEA nanowires can still maintain good flow stress and ductility prior to failure.
Further examination reveals that simultaneous activation of twining induced plasticity and transformation induced plasticity are responsible for the plasticity at different stages and temperatures.

evidence_spans: Therefore, we have chosen silver (Ag) nanowires which have similar SFEs to the CoNiCrFeMn HEAs.

Therefore, in the current study, we have performed MD simulations on both single element Ag NWs and multicomponent CoNiCrFeMn HEA NWs to investigate their deformation behaviors as they have almost similar stacking fault energies.
To investigate the temperature dependent deformation mechanism during the tensile deformation of CoNiCrFeMn HEA and Ag NWs, we have conducted a series of atomistic simulations at 77, 300, and 1000 K.
The Ag NW consists 47,250 atoms while HEA NW contains 55,216 atoms.
After equilibration, a constant strain rate of 10 8 1/s is applied along the z direction.
During tensile deformation, a canonical or NVT (temperature, volume, and energy are conserved) ensemble is used to maintain temperature in a constant volume environment.
The atomic stress of each atom is calculated using the Virial theorem [ [47] ].
In order to identify the defects nucleated during tensile deformation, the common neighbor analysis as implemented in OVITO [ [48] ] is used.
The partial dislocation movement is responsible for high elongation and ductility of NWs, while FCC-HCP martensitic transformation contributes to the strain hardening behavior [ [21] ].
It was established that plastic behavior of metallic NWs mainly depends upon process of nucleation and propagation of dislocations from free surfaces and their interactions with pre-existing defects.

intervention.description: Deformation via nucleation and propagation of partial dislocation from free surface

structure.description: Transformation from (110) to (100) phase; formation of stacking faults separating into twin boundaries

evidence_units.mechanism: Phase transformation driven by surface stresses enabling reduction in surface energy; twin boundary propagation and growth through entire NW
evidence_spans: At 77 K, Ag NW deforms via nucleation and propagation of a partial dislocation from the free surface, leaving a stacking fault inside the NW (see Figure 3 a).

structure.description: Multiple glide mechanism activated; partial re-orientation from (110) to (100) is limited

evidence_units.mechanism: Thermal vibrations retard propagation of twin boundaries; multiple glide mechanism activated leading to necking
evidence_spans: Eventually, nanowire fails by the necking as the multiple glide mechanism activated at 300 K as shown in Figure 3 b.

structure.description: No re-orientation at cross-section; partial dislocation junctions form

evidence_units.mechanism: Activation of partial dislocations on different slip planes dominates deformation; dislocation slip overrides twinning
evidence_spans: In contrast to this, at 1000 K, there is no re-orientation at the cross-section and nanowire fails due to the necking in the region of partial dislocation junctions due to activation of partial dislocations on different slip planes resulting in a lower elongation to failure (see Figure 3 c).

structure.description: Nucleation of partial dislocation followed by deformation twins; formation of Lomer Cottrell locks

evidence_units.mechanism: Nucleation of partial dislocation leads to deformation twins; interaction of moving dislocations forms Lomer Cottrell locks; accumulation of dislocations and stacking faults results in FCC-HCP martensitic transformation; simultaneous activation of twinning and martensitic transformation delays necking
evidence_spans: After a succession of such events in HEA NW, a remarkable drop in stress indicates the formation of deformation twins (see also Figure 6 ).

structure.description: Multiple partial dislocations nucleate simultaneously at different slip planes; deformation twinning and martensitic transformation to HCP phase

evidence_units.mechanism: Lattice distortion effect amplifies under higher temperatures lowering activation barriers for dislocation nucleation; nucleation and glide of partial dislocations induce twinning and martensitic transformation; reorientation mechanism contributes to extended plasticity until necking
evidence_spans: At 300 K, stress in CoNiCrFeMn HEA NW reaches up to 5.5 GPa at around 5% strain, as shown in Figure 2 b during elastic deformation.

structure.description: Formation of HCP phase sections; unlocking of Lomer Cottrell locks; accumulation of stacking faults

evidence_units.mechanism: Thermal effect raises nucleation frequency; accumulation of stacking faults at Lomer Cottrell locks enables transformation to HCP phase; HCP sections provide secondary reinforcement; necking occurs at HCP phase sections
evidence_spans: Unlike the SS curve of Ag at 1000 K where the flow stress and ductility decay quickly to fulfil the failure, the flow stress of HEA NW can still maintain at a certain degree as good as the flow stress at the low temperature.

structure.description: Complex dislocation network; strong barrier to moving twin boundary; transformation from (110) to (100) between twin boundaries

evidence_units.mechanism: Lomer Cottrell locks form strong barrier to moving twin boundary; multiple synergistic mechanisms activated beginning from partial dislocation nucleation; twinning induced plasticity overtakes at 8% strain; martensitic transformation activates at later stage
evidence_spans: In our simulations at low temperature where dislocation density is high as shown in Figure 7 , Lomer Cottrell locks form a strong barrier to the moving twin boundary shown by black arrows in Figure 6 a.

intervention.description: Deformation at cryogenic temperature for superplasticity

structure.description: Deformation twinning; newly created twin boundaries

evidence_units.mechanism: Deformation twinning maintains elongation with increased work hardening by delaying onset of plastic instability of necking
evidence_spans: In conventional metallic nanowires such as Ag, the operative mechanism for the superplasticity and shape memory effects is deformation twinning, where nucleation and propagation of partial dislocation take place along the NW axis as also shown in Figure 3 a.

structure.description: Complex network of dislocations; limited re-orientation from (110) to (100) due to obstacles

evidence_units.mechanism: Deformation twins interact with dislocations on parallel slip planes creating complex network; lattice distortion and friction limit twinning compared to Ag NW
evidence_spans: However, the complete re-orientation of the nanowire could not take place (see Figure 5 a,b) due to the strong obstacles to the twinning boundary movement from complex dislocation interactions in the form of Lomer Cottrell locks and subsequently from stair rods.
